blocks.text: The eigenvalue lesson introduced the equation Mv = lambda v without dwelling much on v itself. This lesson is entirely about that vector, the eigenvector, the special direction a matrix leaves alone, only stretching or shrinking it, never rotating it to somewhere else.

blocks.alt: A vector multiplied by a matrix, with the result staying on the exact same line through the origin
blocks.caption: This lesson is about exactly which vectors have this property, and why it matters.

blocks.text: 1. What an Eigenvector Actually Is

An eigenvector of a matrix M is any nonzero vector v where Mv lands somewhere on the exact same line through the origin that v was already on, just at a different point along it, possibly further out, possibly closer in, possibly flipped to the other side.

It helps to restate this from the opposite direction too: for almost any matrix and almost any starting vector, applying the matrix rotates that vector onto a new line entirely. Eigenvectors are the narrow, specific exception where no such rotation happens, only a stretch, a shrink, or a flip along the vector own original line.

It is worth emphasizing that eigenvectors describe a property of a specific matrix, not a property of vectors in general. The exact same vector can be a perfectly ordinary, non-special vector for one matrix while being a genuine eigenvector for a completely different matrix, depending entirely on how that particular matrix happens to act on it.

This lesson and the eigenvalue lesson before it are really two halves of one single idea, split apart only so each half could get proper individual attention: the eigenvalue lesson covered the scaling number, this lesson covers the direction that number applies to.
1.1 Finding Eigenvectors By Hand

The formal process rearranges the eigenvalue equation into (M minus lambda I)v = 0, where I is the identity matrix covered in its own lesson. Solving this for v, once lambda is already known, is how eigenvectors are actually derived algebraically, though in practice almost all real code reaches for a library function rather than solving this by hand past the smallest textbook examples.

This rearranged equation also explains why eigenvalues have to be found first, before eigenvectors can be solved for. The equation (M minus lambda I)v = 0 only has a nonzero solution for v when the specific value substituted for lambda is actually one of the matrix true eigenvalues, which is precisely how the eigenvalue-finding step works underneath the library call.

Even without working through the full algebra, it is worth recognizing the shape of the problem: it is a system of linear equations with no unique solution by design, since eigenvectors are only defined up to a scaling factor in the first place, covered earlier in this lesson.
2. Seeing It Geometrically

blocks.alt: A vector v shown before and after being multiplied by matrix M, both lying on the exact same dashed line through the origin
blocks.caption: The transformed vector is longer, but it never left the original line.

blocks.text: This is exactly what makes eigenvectors special among all possible vectors a matrix could be applied to. Nearly every other vector, once multiplied by M, would swing off onto some completely different line. Eigenvectors are the small, specific set that do not.

This picture is worth returning to any time the algebra of eigenvectors starts to feel abstract. Every single equation in this lesson is describing exactly this one visual idea, a vector staying on its own line while everything else about it, its length and possibly its direction along that line, is free to change.
2.1 A Non-Diagonal Example

The examples so far used diagonal matrices specifically because their eigenvectors are obvious by inspection. Most real matrices are not diagonal, and their eigenvectors point in directions that are not simply along the x or y axis.

blocks.alt: A vector v at an angle, transformed by a non-diagonal matrix into a longer vector on the exact same line
blocks.caption: The eigenvector direction here is not aligned with either axis, but the same rule still applies exactly.

code.content:
M = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(M)
print(eigenvalues)      # [3. 1.]
print(eigenvectors)
# [[ 0.707 -0.707]
#  [ 0.707  0.707]]

blocks.text: Neither eigenvector here points purely along x or y, each is a diagonal direction instead, and both still satisfy the exact same defining equation as the simpler diagonal examples did.

It is worth noticing that both eigenvectors of this particular matrix happen to sit at a perfect 45 degree angle to each other, which is not a coincidence, this matrix is symmetric, and symmetric matrices always produce orthogonal eigenvectors, exactly the property named in the next section.

Notice too that both eigenvalues here, 3 and 1, are positive, meaning both special directions get stretched rather than flipped, just by different amounts, 3 times along one diagonal direction and only 1 times, meaning unchanged, along the other.
3. Eigenvectors Are Not Unique in Length

Any scalar multiple of an eigenvector is also an eigenvector for the exact same eigenvalue, since scaling a vector never moves it off its own line through the origin. Because of this, libraries have to pick one specific length to report, and the near-universal convention is returning eigenvectors as unit vectors, magnitude exactly 1, covered in the unit vector lesson.

code.content:
import numpy as np
M = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 3]])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(M)
print(np.linalg.norm(eigenvectors[:, 0]))   # 1.0, already a unit vector

blocks.text: This is precisely why questions like how many eigenvectors does a matrix have are usually better phrased as how many independent eigenvector directions, or equivalently how many distinct eigenvalues, a matrix has, since each direction technically contains infinitely many individual vectors, one for every possible length.

None of this ambiguity in length is a flaw in the definition, it is simply a natural consequence of what an eigenvector actually claims: that a whole line through the origin behaves a certain way, not any one specific point along that line.
3.1 Negative Multiples Count Too

Multiplying an eigenvector by -1 still produces a valid eigenvector for the same eigenvalue, since -v sits on the exact same line through the origin as v, just pointing the opposite way along it. This is why some libraries and textbooks report a given eigenvector with the opposite sign from another, both are equally correct.

A quick way to sanity check two reported eigenvectors that look different is checking whether one is simply a negative or scaled copy of the other, rather than assuming a mismatch means an actual error somewhere in a calculation.
4. Computing Eigenvectors in Code

code.content:
M = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 3]])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(M)
print(eigenvalues)      # [2. 3.]
print(eigenvectors)
# [[1. 0.]
#  [0. 1.]]

blocks.text: Each column of the returned eigenvectors matrix pairs with the matching eigenvalue at the same position. Here the first eigenvector, (1, 0), pairs with eigenvalue 2, and the second, (0, 1), pairs with eigenvalue 3.

It is worth double checking the returned eigenvectors are actually unit length as a sanity check on unfamiliar code or an unfamiliar library, since the specific normalization convention can occasionally differ between tools, even though the underlying direction they describe never does.

code.content:
v = eigenvectors[:, 0]
lam = eigenvalues[0]
print(np.allclose(M.dot(v), lam * v))   # True, confirms the defining equation holds

blocks.text: This same check is worth running on every new matrix encountered for the first time, since it takes only one line and builds direct confidence that the returned eigenvectors genuinely satisfy the definition covered at the very start of this lesson, rather than being trusted purely because a library produced them.
5. A Worked Example By Hand
Verifying the pairing directly confirms the equation from the eigenvalue lesson holds exactly.

code.content:
v = np.array([1, 0])
lam = 2
print(M.dot(v))         # [2. 0.]
print(lam * v)          # [2 0], matches exactly

blocks.text: Doing this verification step by hand, even briefly, is one of the fastest ways to build real confidence in what an eigenvector actually is, rather than treating np.linalg.eig as an opaque black box that simply returns two arrays with no clear relationship between them.

This kind of direct verification is worth making a habit of anytime an eigenvector calculation feeds into something important downstream, since a subtle bug earlier in a pipeline, like accidentally transposing a matrix, often shows up first as this verification quietly failing rather than as an obvious crash.
6. Eigenvectors of Symmetric Matrices Are Orthogonal

Symmetric matrices, covered in the matrix transpose lesson, have a genuinely convenient property: their eigenvectors are always orthogonal to each other, meeting at exactly 90 degrees, covered fully in the orthogonality lesson coming up. This is not true for matrices in general, but it holds reliably for symmetric ones.

blocks.title: Why this specific fact matters so much
blocks.content: Covariance matrices, central to PCA later in this module, are always symmetric, which guarantees their eigenvectors form a clean, perpendicular set of directions, exactly the property PCA relies on to describe data along independent axes.

code.content:
A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
print(np.array_equal(A, A.T))   # True, symmetric
_, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(vecs[:, 0].dot(vecs[:, 1]))   # 0.0 (or extremely close), confirming orthogonality

blocks.text: It is worth being precise about the word guarantee here. For a general, non-symmetric matrix, eigenvectors can still happen to be orthogonal by coincidence, but there is no rule forcing it. Symmetry is what turns this from a coincidence into something you can rely on every single time.

Whenever a matrix in a real project turns out to be symmetric, this orthogonality guarantee is worth actively taking advantage of, since orthogonal directions, covered fully in the next lesson, are unusually easy to reason about compared to directions that overlap or interfere with each other in more complicated ways.
7. Eigenvectors as a New Coordinate System

A full set of eigenvectors for a matrix can be used as an entirely new set of reference directions, an alternative coordinate system built specifically around how that matrix naturally stretches space. Described in these eigenvector-aligned coordinates, the matrix action becomes as simple as it can possibly be, just scaling along each axis independently, with no more complicated mixing between directions at all.

blocks.title: This is exactly what makes PCA work
blocks.content: Rotating a dataset into the coordinate system defined by its covariance matrix eigenvectors is the entire mechanism behind principal component analysis, covered fully later in this module. Once in that rotated system, the data spreads out along independent axes, ranked by how much variance, another word for spread, each one explains.

blocks.text: Picture rotating an entire picture until two specific, perpendicular directions happen to line up with the horizontal and vertical axes of the page. That rotation is exactly what switching into eigenvector coordinates does, and the reason it helps is that whatever process the matrix represents becomes far easier to describe once it lines up cleanly with the new axes.
7.1 A Worked Intuition

Imagine a photo being stretched twice as wide but left the same height. Described in ordinary horizontal and vertical coordinates, that stretch mixes into a slightly awkward description if the photo were rotated first. Described in coordinates aligned with the stretch own natural horizontal and vertical directions, the exact same operation becomes the simplest possible description: multiply one coordinate by 2, leave the other alone. Eigenvector coordinates are exactly this kind of natural alignment, just for whatever specific matrix is being studied.

This is exactly why eigenvector-based techniques are sometimes described as finding the natural axes of a problem, axes that were always implicitly there, waiting to be uncovered, rather than an arbitrary choice imposed on the data from outside.
8. Why Eigenvectors Matter in AI

items: Principal component analysis: the principal components are literally the eigenvectors of a dataset covariance matrix, ranked by their eigenvalues.
Dimensionality reduction: keeping only the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues captures most of the meaningful structure in far fewer dimensions.
Understanding what a transformation does structurally, its eigenvectors reveal the natural axes the transformation is built around.

blocks.text: Both of these examples, PCA and PageRank, share the same underlying shape: a large, complicated system gets reduced down to a small number of directions, or a single dominant one, that summarize the most important structure, which is really the whole promise eigenvectors make across every field they show up in.
8.1 A Second Use: Google PageRank

A famous historical example outside of PCA is the original PageRank algorithm behind early Google search, which ranked web pages using the eigenvector of a giant matrix describing how pages link to each other. The eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue described the long-run, stable importance of each page, a genuinely different application from PCA but built on the exact same underlying mathematical idea covered in this lesson.

This historical example is worth remembering specifically because it shows eigenvectors solving a problem that, on the surface, has nothing to do with geometry or data at all, ranking the importance of web pages, which is a good reminder that this mathematical idea generalizes far beyond the geometric pictures used to build intuition for it in this lesson.
9. A Worked Example

code.content:
A = np.array([[4, 0], [0, -1]])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(eigenvalues)     # [4. -1.]
print(eigenvectors)
# [[1. 0.]
#  [0. 1.]]

blocks.text: Working through one more example with slightly less obvious numbers helps confirm the pattern holds generally, not just for the clean, simple matrices used earlier in this lesson.

code.content:
A = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(eigenvalues)      # [1. -1.]
print(eigenvectors)
# [[ 0.707 -0.707]
#  [ 0.707  0.707]]

blocks.text: 10. Practice: Verify This Eigenvector
Given M = [[5, 0], [0, 2]], verify that (1, 0) is an eigenvector, and find its eigenvalue, before checking below.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.content: M times (1, 0) gives (5, 0), which is exactly 5 times (1, 0). The vector stayed on the same line, only scaled, confirming it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 5.

blocks.text: Try one more on your own before moving to the next lesson: for M = [[1, 0], [0, 6]], confirm that (0, 1) is an eigenvector and find its eigenvalue. Following the exact same steps used throughout this lesson, multiplying M by (0, 1), should make the answer immediately clear.
11. Common Mistakes

items: Expecting a specific length from an eigenvector, only its direction, the line it sits on, is actually meaningful.
Assuming any two matrices share the same eigenvectors, they generally do not, each matrix has its own set.
Forgetting that eigenvectors of non-symmetric matrices are not guaranteed to be orthogonal to each other.
Assuming eigenvectors are unique in a strict sense, any nonzero scalar multiple of a valid eigenvector is equally valid.
Trying to find eigenvectors of a non-square matrix, eigenvectors, like eigenvalues, are only defined for square matrices.
Treating the eigenvector output of a library function as an arbitrary black box rather than verifying it satisfies the defining equation directly.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes trace back to the same root cause: treating eigenvectors as ordinary vectors with a fixed, meaningful length, rather than as directions that happen to be reported at a conventional length purely for consistency.
Key Takeaway

An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a matrix leaves on the same line through the origin, only scaling or flipping it, paired with an eigenvalue describing exactly how much. Any scalar multiple of an eigenvector is also one, which is why libraries report them as unit vectors by convention.

Symmetric matrices, including every covariance matrix, have orthogonal eigenvectors, and those eigenvectors are literally what PCA calls its principal components, ranked by eigenvalue, which is exactly why this lesson and the eigenvalue lesson before it are the direct foundation the PCA lesson later in this module is built on.

Carrying the picture of a vector sliding along its own fixed line, rather than the raw algebra alone, is the single most useful thing to take from this lesson into the eigenvalue-heavy topics still ahead in this module.
